meters.label: High-level files edited by a provider swap

frames.narration: First version: OrderService creates an SmtpMailer and a database inside its own constructor. It works, and it is the shortest code. The arrow points from the rule down to the detail.
A test of the order rule cannot avoid the mailer and the database: every test sends real mail and writes real rows. All 11 tests of the codebase need real infrastructure.
The company changes mail provider, with a different API. Invoices and reminders also create their own mailer, so three services that hold business rules must be opened, edited and re-tested.

Inversion starts by giving the policy an interface, owned by it and in its own words: notify a customer. It is not named after SMTP and has no host or port. The policy now depends on its own abstraction.
The detail now depends on the policy's interface: SmtpMailer implements Notifier. The arrow that used to point down points up. That reversal is the inversion.
Someone has to choose the real implementation. The composition root creates SmtpMailer and passes it in. That handing-in is dependency injection, the technique, and it is separate from the principle.
A test passes a fake notifier that stores messages in a list. The rule runs in memory, in microseconds. Only the 2 integration tests of the adapters still need real infrastructure.

The provider changes again. Only the adapter is rewritten and the composition root names the new class. OrderService, InvoiceService and ReminderService are not edited. The trap is an interface named IMailer with host and port: that one would still leak SMTP into the policy.
